pages.summary: A sparse matrix: only the nonzero elements stored, with their places.
body: Most elements of the matrices from networks, grids and finite elements are zero; a sparse matrix stores just the others, so a matrix with a million rows and a few nonzeros in each fits easily, and products and solves skip the zeros. `sparse(i, j, v)` puts `v(k)` at row `i(k)`, column `j(k)`, adding the values given for one place. Sparse results stay sparse where zeros stay zero: sums and products of sparse matrices, `S'`, indexing, comparisons, and functions such as `abs`, `sqrt`, `sum` and `kron`. Combined with a full matrix (`S + A`, `S*A`, `S\b`) or a nonzero number (`S + 1`), the result is full.
syntax: From row indices, column indices and values.
S = sparse(i, j, v, m, n)

body: `full` stores every element, zeros included; it leaves a full matrix as it is. `issparse` is true for sparse storage, whatever the number of zeros.

body: `spones` keeps a matrix's pattern and replaces each nonzero by 1, which is how to count or draw the structure.

pages.summary: The room for nonzero elements, and an all-zero matrix with room for some.
body: Here a sparse matrix grows its storage as elements are added, so `spalloc(m, n, nz)` is an all-zero m-by-n matrix (`nz`, the number of nonzeros expected, is taken but not needed) and `nzmax` is the number of nonzeros (at least 1).

pages.summary: Random sparse matrices with a given density of nonzeros.
body: `sprand` draws the nonzeros from the uniform distribution on (0, 1), `sprandn` from the standard normal; `density` is the share of nonzero elements (somewhat fewer when random places coincide). `sprandsym` makes a symmetric one with normal values, or one with the pattern of a given matrix.

examples.title: Their densities and values

pages.summary: A sparse matrix built from diagonals, or the diagonals taken out of a matrix.
body: `spdiags(B, d, m, n)` puts column k of `B` on diagonal `d(k)` (0 the main one, positive above, negative below). When m >= n, as for a square matrix, a diagonal above the main one takes the last elements of its column and one below takes the first. `spdiags(B, d, A)` replaces diagonals of `A`; `[B, d] = spdiags(A)` gives back every nonzero diagonal.
syntax: An m-by-n matrix from the columns of `B`.
The nonzero diagonals and their numbers.

Which elements of a column land on the diagonal

pages.summary: A function applied to the nonzero elements of a sparse matrix only.
body: The zeros stay zero and the result stays sparse, which matters for functions such as `exp` that would turn every zero into something else.

pages.summary: A sparse matrix from rows of [i j v] (or [i j re im] for complex values).
body: The form sparse matrices are often written to text files in: a row for each nonzero, with its row, column and value. A last row `[m n 0]` sets the size.

examples.title: Read from rows, with the size set by the last

pages.summary: The augmented matrix [c*I A; A' 0] of a least-squares problem.
body: Least squares as one square sparse system: `[c*I A; A' 0]*[r/c; x] = [b; 0]` gives the residual `r = b - A*x` and the least-squares solution `x`. `c` is 1 unless given.

examples.title: Least squares through the augmented system

pages.summary: The sparse solvers' settings, kept and read back.
body: The settings (such as `'spumoni'`, `'thr_rel'`, `'umfpack'`) can be set, read and reset as a whole, but the sparse solvers here keep their own: changing them changes no result.

pages.summary: A dot at each nonzero element of a matrix: its sparsity pattern.
body: The rows run down and the columns across, as the matrix is written; the x-label gives the number of nonzeros.

examples.title: The five-point Laplacian on an 8-by-8 grid

pages.summary: Orderings of a symmetric matrix that keep its Cholesky factor sparse.
body: Reordering the rows and columns together, `S(p, p)`, changes how much fill a factorization creates. `symrcm` (reverse Cuthill-McKee) brings the nonzeros close to the diagonal, giving a narrow band; `amd` and `symamd` (approximate minimum degree) aim at the fewest nonzeros in the factor.

examples.title: A shuffled grid matrix, reordered

pages.summary: Column orderings for sparse LU and QR factorizations.
body: For a factorization of `A(:, q)`, the fill depends on the order of the columns. `colamd` orders them by approximate minimum degree on the pattern of `A'*A` (whose Cholesky factor is the R of QR); `colperm` simply puts the columns with fewest nonzeros first.
syntax: By the number of nonzeros in each column.

examples.title: Fewer nonzeros in R

pages.summary: A maximum matching of columns to rows, and the structural rank.
body: From the pattern alone, not the values: `dmperm(A)` gives for each column the row matched to it (0 for none), as many as possible with no row used twice; `sprank` is the number matched, an upper bound on the rank that the values may lower.
syntax: The row matched to each column.

examples.title: Two columns compete for one row

pages.summary: The elimination tree of a symmetric matrix, and the structure of its Cholesky factor.
body: Without factoring: `etree(A)` gives the parent of each column in the tree that says which columns of the Cholesky factor depend on which (0 for a root); `symbfact` gives the number of nonzeros in each row of the factor, the tree's height, the parents, a postorder and the factor's pattern. They tell in advance how much room and work a factorization takes.
syntax: The nonzeros in each row of the factor.
With the height, parents, postorder and pattern.

examples.title: The tree of a grid matrix, and the factor's counts
examples.code:
A = gallery('poisson', 3);
p = etree(A)
count = symbfact(A)'
full(sum(chol(A) ~= 0, 2))'
treeplot(p)

pages.summary: The incomplete Cholesky factorization: L*L' close to A, with L kept sparse.
body: A full Cholesky factor of a sparse matrix fills in; the incomplete one keeps `L` to `A`'s pattern (`'nofill'`), or drops the entries smaller than a tolerance (`'ict'` with `droptol`), so that `L*L'` is only close to `A`. It is a preconditioner: `pcg(A, b, tol, maxit, L, L')` converges in far fewer steps. `A` must be symmetric positive definite (read from its lower triangle); `michol` makes `L*L'` keep `A`'s row sums, and `diagcomp` factors `A + alpha*diag(diag(A))` when the plain one breaks down.

examples.title: No fill against the full factor
A drop tolerance

pages.summary: The incomplete LU factorization: L*U close to A, with L and U kept sparse.
body: The preconditioner for nonsymmetric systems, as `ichol` is for symmetric ones: `'nofill'` keeps `A`'s pattern, `'crout'` and `'ilutp'` drop the entries smaller than `droptol` (relative to each column's norm), and `'ilutp'` also pivots. Given to `gmres` or `bicgstab` as `M1 = L` and `M2 = U`. With one output, `L + U - I` in one matrix.

examples.title: A preconditioner for gmres

without: flag 0 after 224 steps
with ilu: flag 0 after 28 steps
